Method, assumptions & limits

Concept-sizing estimate: a 2D plate conduction model coupled to 1D channel hydraulics. Expect roughly ±15–30 % compared with CFD or test data, and validate final designs by simulation or measurement.

  • Heat transfer. Laminar: Shah & London NuH1 and f·Re for the channel aspect ratio, with a Hausen-type entry correction per straight pass. Turbulent: Gnielinski with a short-duct correction. Re 2300–4000 is blended. Bends restart the boundary layer; Dean-vortex enhancement is ignored (conservative).
  • 2D plate model. The plate face is a grid of up to about 6,000 cells conducting in-plane through the local solid thickness. Cells above channels, port leads and headers are coupled to the coolant through the heated-face wall and the fin-corrected convective film. The coolant is marched along each channel path until plate and coolant agree. This gives the map, the peak temperature and the component temperatures.
  • Components. Case = plate under the footprint + P·(t/k + contact resistance)/A of the TIM. Junction = case + P·Rjc. Spreading through the plate thickness under small sources is not modelled, so very small, intense sources read slightly optimistic.
  • Pressure drop. Shah apparent friction (laminar, developing) and Haaland (turbulent); Darby 3-K for 180° bends; fixed loss coefficients for channel entry/exit (0.5 + 1.0) and ports (1.5 each).
  • Flow distribution. Parallel layouts: the headers are split into segments with friction and momentum (the inlet header regains 1.0×, the outlet header loses 2.0× the velocity-head change), balanced against each channel's own Δp(q). The per-channel flows set the header losses and each channel's heat transfer in the 2D model.
  • Pump curve. The operating flow is found by bisection where the pump pressure rise equals the plate plus rest-of-loop pressure drop (which scales with flow²).
  • Fluids. Properties at the mean bulk temperature. Glycol data by volume, approximate (±5–10 %). Gases are ideal and incompressible within the plate, at inlet pressure.
  • Not modelled. Radiation and natural convection, two-phase flow, turbulators and pin fins, gas compressibility within the plate.
  • Transient load: implicit (backward-Euler) time stepping of the same 2D plate model with the heat capacity of the plate and, optionally, of each component; the coolant is treated as quasi-steady because it passes through the plate in a fraction of a second. Junction-to-case and TIM layers have no heat capacity, so their share of a load change appears at once (conservative).

Cold Plate Calculator

Version 2 · by Eren Tozlu

A free, browser-based tool for first-pass sizing of liquid- and gas-cooled cold plates for power electronics, batteries and fuel-cell systems. It couples a 2D conduction model of the plate with 1D channel hydraulics, pump matching and manifold flow distribution. All calculations run in your browser.

Made by Eren Tozlu. More engineering tools and projects at ehcrea.com.

Open source under the MIT License; the source code is on GitHub.

Enjoying the calculator? It is free for everyone and I keep adding features in my spare time. If it saved you time on a project or helped you learn, you can support its development on Patreon. Every contribution, big or small, helps me keep building new engineering tools. Thank you!

How to use

Work through the inputs on the left from top to bottom; the results on the right update as you type.

  1. Start from an example. Pick an application preset in the toolbar and adapt it. You can switch SI/Imperial units and the language at any time.
  2. Plate. Length, width, thickness and material. Higher conductivity spreads heat better between the channels.
  3. Flow layout. Serpentine: one long channel (or a few circuits), even cooling but higher pressure drop. Parallel Z/U: many short channels fed by headers, low pressure drop; check the flow distribution card.
  4. Channel section. Round, square or rectangular. Channel depth plus the heated-face wall must fit within the plate thickness.
  5. Coolant. Fluid, inlet temperature and pressure, and either a fixed flow rate or a pump curve; with a pump curve the operating point is found automatically.
  6. Heat input. Uniform heat: enter a power to get the peak temperature, or a maximum surface temperature to get the capacity. Heat sources: add components with power, footprint, TIM and Rjc, and drag them on the plate layout.

Reading the results

  • The headline shows the capacity, peak temperature or hottest junction. Warnings and notes point out design problems.
  • Hover over the 2D map to read local temperatures. The component table lists plate, case and junction temperatures with the margin to each limit.
  • The breakdown bars show which thermal resistance or pressure loss dominates: improve the largest one first.
  • Transient load shows how temperatures develop during an overload, a cold start or pulses, and how long a load can last before a limit is reached.
  • Size for a target finds the lowest flow, fewest channels, thinnest plate or warmest coolant that meets your limit. Parameter sweep shows how one input affects the result; Design comparison puts saved variants side by side.
  • The step-by-step calculation shows every formula with your numbers.

Typical values

  • Channel velocity for water/glycol: 0.5–2 m/s (aluminium ≲ 2 m/s against erosion).
  • Coolant temperature rise: 3–10 K for good temperature uniformity.
  • TIM: thermal grease ≈ 0.05–0.2 K·cm²/W, gap pads ≈ 1–5 K·cm²/W.

Saving and sharing

Your design is saved in this browser automatically. Copy link creates a URL with all inputs, Export PDF writes a design report including the calculation steps, and Print prints the page.

Results are engineering estimates for concept sizing (about ±15–30 %). Validate final designs by CFD or test.
